4301.text: Jer.21.7 and Jer.46.26 both use the idiom 'those who seek their life/lives' -- here the base sense of seeking shifts to a lethal-intent nuance (seeking in order to kill), the Hebraism explicitly noted in the meaning tree as carried over into Greek zeteo; this is a marked intensification compared to the neutral or benevolent seeking senses elsewhere in the batch, showing the same root can denote mortal hostility when combined with 'life/soul' as object.

4308.text: M47 (life, H5315H) co-occurs in Jer.46.26 in the same hostile-pursuit idiom as Jer.21.7; seeking is the pursuing action, life/soul is its object -- the two terms combine into the fixed idiom but remain distinct characteristics.

5492.text: In 2 Chr 15:13 darash carries its well-attested devotional sense 'seek the Lord' -- this is within the base gloss's own listed sub-sense (1a3, seeking deity in prayer/worship), not a divergence from it; contrast with the necromantic-object occurrences shows the same verb pivoting entirely on its object rather than on any special contextual nuance of the verb form itself.

5498.text: In 2 Chr 15:13 the operation 'put to death' (H4191, role-T3) is directed by the covenant community against whoever fails to seek the Lord; the seeking itself (H1875) is the required act of the individual party directed toward the Lord/God of Israel, and its absence triggers the death-operation against that same individual.

6547.text: In Ps.37.25 'begging' renders baqash for a child seeking bread out of want, a specific nuance of desperate physical need rather than the more common senses of hostile pursuit or devotional seeking found elsewhere (e.g. Ps.27.4, Ps.35.4); the impact here is to underscore God's providence toward the righteous by contrast, since such begging is said never to be observed.

6560.text: Other M-codes present in Ps.37.25: M12 (righteous), M30/M59 (forsaken). Baqash (begging) describes the hypothetical desperate act of a righteous person's child; it stands in negated contrast to being forsaken (M30/M59), illustrating what does NOT happen to the righteous (M12), but does not itself modify those terms.

14187.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Anger lodges, and where it lodges is named. "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools" (Ecc 7:9). This joins Job 36:13 ("cherish anger"). Anger that stays has a lodging, and the lodging is the fool's. The verse before sets up the pair: "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" (7:8); Its duration is limited to a day: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil" (Eph 4:26–27). Where Gen 27 waited years for anger to turn away, the NT sets a limit of one day. The reason given is what anger left overnight opens: "opportunity to the devil"; It repeats: "A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again" (Pro 19:19). Great wrath is a pattern, not an event. Rescue does not end it; It is weighed:; "A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both" (Pro 27:3). This echoes Job's "heavier than the sand of the sea"; "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?" (Pro 27:4). Anger is measured, and jealousy is found to be worse; Jealousy makes it unappeasable: "jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation" (Pro 6:34–35). This is the one anger in Proverbs that a gift will not avert. Compare §23: "A gift in secret averts anger" (Pro 21:14); It shows at once: "The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult" (Pro 12:16). The fool's anger cannot be hidden, while the prudent one lets the insult pass unanswered; It is where the wicked end up: "the expectation of the wicked [ends] in wrath".

14208.text: How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.

14217.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The one wronged is now God, or God's law, rather than a sister, a friend or the poor: The indignation seizes its bearer: "Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law" (Psa 119:53). The bearer is its object as well as its subject. It is framed between comfort in God's rules (119:52) and "Your statutes have been my songs" (119:54). The indignation sits inside a life held by the law it defends; The spirit provoked by what it sees: "while Paul was waiting … his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue … and in the marketplace every day" (Act 17:16–17). This is the same movement as Neh 5:6–7: indignation, then an inner act, then public speech. Here the seat is named in the indignation verse itself; Annoyance that finally acts: the slave girl "kept doing this for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you … come out of her'" (Act 16:18); What annoys him is a true proclamation ("These men are servants of the Most High God", 16:17) from a wrong source; The anger builds over "many days" before the act; The act sets off anger in others: "when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas" (16:19).

15094.text: Worn. "The Lord reigns; he is robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2).

15109.text: What the batch 1 verses state: The same words are used of God and of people. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh name God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18). So yes: these words describe a characteristic of God. In ESV English the difference shows in the choice of word ("majesty" against "pride"), not in the Hebrew; God's majesty is his own and is not taken on. He is "robed in majesty" while "you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). Nothing in these verses shows it being acquired. It is shown in acts: the sea, the overthrow, the thunder; It is challenged, but it is not overturned. The researcher's word "undisputed" needs one qualification from the verses. God's majesty is disputed: by the enemy at the sea (Exo 15:9), by "all that is proud and lofty" (Isa 2:12), and by the one who says "I will ascend to heaven" (Isa 14:13). Each time the dispute ends with the one who rose brought down. So it is not uncontested; it is never overturned; Majesty goes with what only God can do. Job 40:10–14 makes the test plain: whoever wears majesty must abase every proud one and save by his own hand. Only God does; Human pride in these verses is mostly a standing that is taken, or kept against God; It is said in the heart against the facts: "the bricks have fallen, but we will build" (Isa 9:10); It is worn as a show (Psa 73:6); It is set over the weak (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25); It refuses to hear (Jer 13:15–17); It stands on might and strongholds (Lev 26:19; Amo 6:8; Eze 33:26); This agrees with the researcher's "mostly assumed"; But the same word for people is not always assumed. God gives a "pride" to his people: chosen (Psa 47:4), given (Isa 4:2), made (Isa 60:15), restored (Nah 2:2). The Lord himself is their "triumph" (Deu 33:29). The verses also show a given honour turned into pride (Eze 7:20; 24:21); I read: the line the verses draw is not between God having majesty and people having none. It runs between a standing that is one's own by nature (God), a standing given by God (his people), and a standing taken, or turned against the giver (pride); The Son's majesty is described as received, and it stands beside his being handed over; "he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17); "after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" (Heb 1:3); At the very moment of "the majesty of God", he speaks of being "delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44); This joins 13.1 Lowering himself (M09): the one with majesty did not hold onto it in the way pride holds; I read: where Php 2:6–9 joins the two, it lies outside this batch's words; A majesty that depends on people is the contrast. Artemis's "magnificence" can be "deposed", because it rests on "she whom all Asia and the world worship" (Act 19:27). I read: this is the borrowed standing that pride is, set against God's majesty, which no one confers.

15195.text: The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

16038.text: 9. Cross-cutting observations for Batch B [Claude reading]: The heart is the organ of attention, knowing, understanding, storing, remembering and reasoning. Attention is literally *setting the heart*. The heart's hardness is the same thing as failing to hear and understand.; The soul relates to knowledge by *receiving* it (pleasant, sweet, life-giving) and by dwelling on memories (bowed down). The soul can be commanded to remember. Soul-desire can run ahead of knowledge.; The human spirit is the seat of self-knowledge and searching. It knows a person's thoughts, makes understanding possible as God's breath in man, searches after the heart meditates, and perceives others' inner reasoning. A cool spirit (temper) is linked with understanding and restrained speech.; God's Spirit is the true source of knowledge, wisdom, skill, teaching, remembrance and prophecy. The heart or own spirit as a source of prophecy is condemned.; Hearing is the main channel into the inner seat. The ear receives; the heart keeps, understands or refuses. News makes hearts melt, spirits revive and souls refresh. God hears the heart. The "hearing heart" of 1 Kgs 3:9 is confirmed in the tags.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the context reads add two qualifications.; Hearing sometimes needs seeing. Jacob's spirit revives only when he sees the wagons (Gen 45:27, Batch G §2). Elisha receives the spirit on condition of seeing (2Ki 2:10, Batch F §9.5).; What is heard moves between people. 16491.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

16492.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)

For he has delivered the life of the needy" (13); → "Cursed be the day on which I was born!" (14); Jer 11:18–21 has the same prayer, and names "the men of Anathoth, who seek your life" (21).; [Claude reading]; Vengeance changes value with the heart that holds it. In the Philistines' soul it is malice. In God's heart it stands in one line with redemption (Isa 63:4). 16988.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch F [Claude reading]: Relating to others is most often a matter of the soul.; Souls are knit (1Sa 18:1).; A soul loves, seeks and fails (Song 3; 5).; Malice lives in the soul (Eze 25:6, 15).; Souls abhor each other, even God's soul and the people's (Lev 26).; One loves another "as one's own soul".; The heart is where hatred starts and is spoken (Lev 19:17; Gen 27:41). It is also where the response to another's fall is judged (Pro 24:17).; The human spirit registers bonds and bearing.; It is unsettled by a friend's absence and refreshed by a friend's arrival (2Co 2:13; 7:13; 1Co 16:18).; It is the manner of approach — gentleness (1Co 4:21).; It is what the wise hold back and the fool vents (Pro 29:11).; Sequences matter more than single verses. Reading before and after changed the picture in six places: 1Sa 18 (Jonathan and Saul); Lev 26 (reciprocal abhorrence broken by God); Psa 143 and Psa 51 (the crushing chains); Judg 19 and the other merry-heart narratives (threshold states); 2Co 2 → 7 (the spirit's rest through persons); 2Ki 2 (spirit transfer confirmed by others); Meaning shifts with circumstance in consistent ways: *crush*: by whom, and turned to whom (§5); *tender heart*: to what it yields (§6); *good heart*: from God or from wine (§7); *love / hate one's soul*: well-being vs clinging (§3); *hāgâ*: what the heart rehearses (§12.2); *nûaḥ*: what rests in or on the person (§9.5); Inner states spread between people: the fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8); heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42); a lowly heart gives rest to other souls (Mat 11:29); a congregation refreshes Titus's spirit (2Co 7:13); the prophet's heart takes in the people's doom (Jer 4:18–19); Other spirits relate to people as occupants of a house (Mat 12:43–45) and as seizures between people (1Sa 18:10; Judg 9:23 in Batch D). The divine Spirit rests upon people and is recognised by others (Num 11; 2Ki 2).; Fringe worth keeping: the knit soul beside the seizing spirit in one chapter (1Sa 18); the heart awake while the body lags (Song 5); God refusing to complete reciprocal abhorrence (Lev 26:44); Jezebel curing a vexed spirit by a manufactured good heart (1Ki 21); the prophet's heart for Moab set against Ammon's malice of soul (Isa 15; Jer 48; Eze 25); past hatred as a legal criterion (Deu 19)

16995.text: 0. Data notes: Pre-filters from the handoff do not apply here. None of "Holy Spirit" (M61), "declares the Lord" (M42) or "Lord of hosts" (M72) falls in Batch C clusters. Nothing was removed.; "Seek my life" is one idiom, not inner seeking. About 40 of the 96 M83 verses are *biqqēš nephesh* — "seek (someone's) life" (1Sa 20:1; 23:15; 1Ki 19:10, 14; Jer 11:21; 19:7; 21:7; 22:25; 34:20–21; 44:30; 46:26; 49:37; Psa 35:4; 38:12; 40:14; 54:3; 63:9; 70:2; 86:14; Mat 2:20; Rom 11:3; etc.). Here *nephesh* is life as the object of hostile pursuit. It is reported in §7.5 and not mixed with the soul that seeks.; "Lacks sense" is "lacking heart" (H2638 + H3820A, d1): Pro 7:7; 9:4, 16; 10:13, 21; 11:12; 12:11; 15:21; 17:18; 24:30; 6:32; Ecc 10:3. H2638 "lacking" is filed under M18 Desire. It is a lack, not a desire. See §1.5. → Ruling R1.; "Pleasant" (H2896A *ṭôv*) is mostly generic "good / better". It accounts for 59 M18 pairs. The inner-being uses ("glad / merry / good of heart", "good to the soul", "better … in spirit") are kept in §1.6. Generic "better" is noted and not used (Num 11:18; Judg 9:2; Dan 1:15; 2Sa 18:3; Gen 1:21).; "Striving after wind" (H7469 *reʿût rûaḥ* "longing/pursuit" + rûaḥ *wind*, d1) is the Ecclesiastes refrain (Ecc 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6; 6:9). It is correctly a desire + wind pairing. See §1.9.; "Whole heart" is *lēv shālēm* (H8003 "complete", d1). It is filed under M34 Patience. In the verses it means an undivided, integral heart, not endurance. See §5.1. → Ruling R2.; "Contrite" (H1793A) is filed under M11 Turning. The verses are about a crushed spirit and heart (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15), not about turning. They are kept in §8.4. → Ruling R3.; Misfiled tags, noted and not used: H6569 "refuse" = *dung*, read as "refuse" (M30): the flesh-skin-dung-burned sacrificial verses (Exo 29:14; Lev 4:11; 8:17; 16:27; Num 19:5); also Eze 32:5 "carcass" and Job 41:23 "folds of his flesh".; H0014 "be willing" filed under M30 because it appears as "would not" (1Ch 11:19; 2Sa 23:17 "he would not drink it"). It is kept only where it is the heart's or spirit's refusal (Exo 10:27; Deu 2:30; Eze 3:7).; "As you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2Ki 2:2, 4, 6; 4:30): an oath formula. H5800A "leave" → M30.; Gen 2:24 "leave … one flesh" → M30.

17016.text: The merry heart made vulnerable by wine: "Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk" (1Sa 25:36); "when Amnon's heart is merry with wine … strike Amnon" (2Sa 13:28); "when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded" (Est 1:10); "when their hearts were merry, they said, 'Call Samson'" (Judg 16:25); [Claude reading] Four narratives in which a wine-merry heart is the moment of exposure or rash command.; Revisit 2026-09-28: with before/after context and five further instances (Judg 19:6, 9, 22; Rut 3:7; 1Ki 21:7; Luk 12:19), this is a threshold pattern. After food and wine the good heart lowers guard, and what enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder, anger, catastrophe, outrage, redemption (Ruth), a dead heart next morning (Nabal), God's claim on the soul (Luk 12:20). See Batch F §7.

17073.text: Positive flesh-heart: "written … with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human [*fleshly*] hearts" (2Co 3:3) [D1]. This echoes the "heart of flesh" of Eze 36:26 (§8.3).

17083.text: Measured against David: "his heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father" (1Ki 11:4; 15:3); "the heart of Asa was wholly true to the Lord all his days" (1Ki 15:14; 2Ch 15:17)

17135.text: 8.2 The heart turning away: "lest his heart turn away" (Deu 17:17); "that his heart may not be lifted up … that he may not turn aside" (Deu 17:20); "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "Cursed is the man who … makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5) — heart turning and trusting flesh are the same act; "this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside" (Jer 5:23); "Let not your heart turn aside to her ways" (Pro 7:25); "his wives turned away his heart after other gods" (1Ki 11:4); "their whoring heart that has departed from me" (Eze 6:9); "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jer 32:40) — God guards the heart against turning; "keep your soul diligently … lest they depart from your heart" (Deu 4:9); "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds … they rebel against me" (Hos 7:14).

17136.text: 8.3 God removes and replaces — heart, spirit and flesh in one act: "I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh" (Eze 11:19; 36:26) [H1]; "remove the foreskin of your hearts" (Jer 4:4)

17139.text: 8.3 God removes and replaces — heart, spirit and flesh in one act: [Claude reading] In Eze 11:19 / 36:26, heart, spirit and flesh are all tagged "remove" within four positions. Flesh is the good material here (a "heart of flesh") and stone is the bad, the reverse of NT flesh-desire (§1.11). Compare 2Co 3:3 (§3.3).

17174.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch C [Claude reading]: The soul is the desiring self. In the OT, *nephesh* is the ordinary subject of "want / crave / long / thirst", from appetite for meat (Deu 12:20) to thirst for God (Psa 42:1–2). The same *nephesh* is the life that enemies seek (§7.5) and the life that is precious (§1.7). Desire and vitality are one word.; The heart is where orientation is set, held, divided or hardened. It plans, forms intentions, resolves, seeks, turns, is whole or not whole, and is stubborn or hardened. Many of these are expressed as setting / directing / inclining the heart (1Sa 7:3; Jos 24:23; 2Ch 19:3; 30:19). This extends Batch B's "attention = setting the heart" into will.; The human spirit carries energy and disposition, more than choice. It is "moved" to give (Exo 35:21), "fervent" (Rom 12:11), "willing" against weak flesh (Mat 26:41), patient or proud (Ecc 7:8), ruled (Pro 16:32), hardened with the heart (Deu 2:30), not faithful (Psa 78:8), and crushed or contrite (Psa 34:18; 51:17). Planning and choosing are rarely predicated of the human spirit [observation, not a count].; Heart and spirit are paired in the orientation verses (Exo 35:21; Deu 2:30; Psa 51:17; 78:8; Isa 57:15; Eze 11:19; 36:26). Heart and soul are paired in the "all your heart and all your soul" formula for seeking and returning (Deu 4:29; 1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 15:12).; Flesh changes role across the corpus.; OT: flesh longs and faints for God with the soul (Psa 63:1; 84:2). The "heart of flesh" is God's gift (Eze 36:26).; NT: flesh is the main subject of wrong desire (Gal 5:16–17; 1Jo 2:16), set against the Spirit and the soul (1Pe 2:11) and weak beside a willing spirit (Mat 26:41).; 2Co 3:3 ("tablets of fleshly hearts") keeps the OT positive use inside the NT.; God's Spirit relates to orientation as giver and as the one resisted.; Giver: good Spirit leading (Psa 143:10), patience (Gal 5:22), hope (Rom 5:5; 15:13), received on repentance (Act 2:38).; Resisted: rebelled against and grieved (Isa 63:10), disregarded (1Th 4:8), bypassed in plans (Isa 30:1).; The Spirit also desires against the flesh (Gal 5:17) and wills (1Co 12:11).

17225.text: Seat links that do not count as an inner-being seat: ruach is the day's wind (Gen 3:8, the only seat link of chava, hide); basar is meat (Exo 16:8, the only link of lun, grumble); the divine Spirit speaks (Rev 2:17, the only link of kruptō); a heart belonging to another person (2 Chr 22:9).

17235.text: c. Inner speech — the heart as the place one "says" things: "Said in his heart / to himself": Gen 17:17; 24:45; 27:41; 1Ki 12:26; 1Sa 27:1; Deu 7:17; 8:17; 9:4; 18:21; Psa 10:6, 11, 13; 14:1; 53:1; Isa 14:13; 47:8, 10; 49:21; Jer 5:24; 13:22; Obd 3; Zep 1:12; 2:15; Est 6:6; Ecc 1:16; 2:1, 15; 3:17–18; Rom 10:6; Rev 18:7.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1Sa 1:13).; "Before I had finished speaking in my heart" (Gen 24:45).; The *content* of heart-speech is often self-assessment or self-deception: "I shall not be moved" (Psa 10:6); "There is no God" (Psa 14:1); "My power … has gotten me this wealth" (Deu 8:17); "I am, and there is no one besides me" (Isa 47:8; Zep 2:15).; Nehemiah "took counsel with *myself*" (Neh 5:7, lēv); "Ask *yourself*" style reflexives also appear.

17236.text: d. Thinking, planning, understanding, remembering: *Plans and devising:* Pro 16:1, 9; 19:21; 6:14, 18; 24:2; 12:20; Psa 140:2; 58:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17; Isa 10:7; Act 5:4; Eze 38:10.; *Understanding and knowing:*; "a heart to understand" (Deu 29:4); "understanding mind" (1Ki 3:9); "understand with their hearts" (Isa 6:10; Mat 13:15; Joh 12:40; Act 28:27); "an intelligent heart acquires knowledge" (Pro 18:15); "the heart of the hasty will understand" (Isa 32:4); *Remembering and "laying to heart":*; Isa 47:7; 57:1, 11; 42:25; Mal 2:2; Jer 12:11; Ecc 7:2; 9:1; Deu 4:39; 32:46; 1Sa 21:12; "call to mind" (Lam 3:21; Deu 30:1); "come into mind" (Jer 3:16; 7:31; 19:5; 32:35; 44:21; 51:50; Isa 65:17); Haggai's repeated "Consider your ways" is literally *set your heart* (Hag 1:5, 7; 2:15, 18) [lexical].; *Searching and investigating:* "I applied my heart to seek and to search out" (Ecc 1:13, 17; 7:25; 8:9, 16); "great searchings of heart" (Judg 5:15–16).; *Pondering and treasuring:* Mary "treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luk 2:19, 51); "ponder in your own hearts on your beds" (Psa 4:4); "the meditation of my heart" (Psa 19:14; 49:3).; *Questioning and reasoning:* Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 3:15; 5:22; 9:47; 24:38.

17238.text: f. Feeling: *Joy and gladness:* 1Ki 8:66; Pro 15:13, 15; 27:9, 11; Psa 4:7; 13:5; 16:9; 19:8; 28:7; 33:21; Zep 3:14; Joh 16:22.; *Merriment with wine:* Est 1:10; 2Sa 13:28; Rut 3:7; Judg 16:25; 19:6, 22.; *Sorrow and anguish:* Neh 2:2; Rom 9:2; 2Co 2:4; Joh 16:6; Psa 13:2; 55:4; Lam 1:20; 5:15.; *Fear and melting:* Gen 42:28; 1Sa 28:5; Deu 20:3, 8; Jos 7:5; Isa 7:2; 13:7; 21:4; 35:4; Jer 4:9; Nah 2:10.; *Courage:* Psa 27:14; 31:24; 2Sa 7:27; 17:10; Eze 22:14; Amo 2:16; Psa 76:5; plus the NT compounds "take heart" (Mat 9:2, 22; 14:27; Mar 6:50; 10:49; Joh 16:33; Act 23:11) and "lose heart" (Luk 18:1; 2Co 4:1, 16; Eph 3:13; Gal 6:9; 2Th 3:13).; *Desire:* "the desires of your heart" (Psa 37:4); "heart's desire" (Psa 21:2; 20:4; Rom 10:1).; *Love, attachment, contempt, hate:*; "the king's heart went out to Absalom" (2Sa 14:1); "my heart goes out to the commanders" (Judg 5:9); "your heart is not with me" (Judg 16:15); "I hold you in my heart" (Phili 1:7); "you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2Co 7:3); "despised him in her heart" (2Sa 6:16); "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Lev 19:17); *Grief felt in the heart as physical pain:* "My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly" (Jer 4:19); "My heart throbs" (Psa 38:10); "my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast" (Psa 22:14).

17239.text: g. Moral character and orientation: *Qualities:* pure, upright, blameless, whole, perfect (1Ki 8:61; 15:14; Psa 24:4; 73:1; Mat 5:8; 2Ti 2:22); crooked, perverse, evil, deceitful, proud, haughty, stubborn (Pro 11:20; 17:20; 16:5; Jer 17:9; Jer 7:24 and the "stubbornness of their evil heart" series; Eze 28:2, 17; Obd 3).; *Direction:*; turns (1Ki 11:3–4, 9; Deu 29:18; 30:17), inclines (Psa 119:36, 112; 141:4; Jos 24:23; Judg 9:3), goes after (Eze 11:21; 20:16; 33:31; Job 31:7), is set on (Psa 62:10; Dan 11:28); is near or far (Isa 29:13; Mat 15:8; Mar 7:6); is "toward" someone (1Ch 29:18; 2Ch 16:9); "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Mat 6:21; Luk 12:34); *Whole vs divided:* "with all their heart / whole heart" (many verses; e.g. Psa 119:2, 10, 34, 58, 69, 145; 138:1; Jer 24:7; 29:13; 2Ch 15:15; 31:21); "not with a whole heart" (2Ch 25:2); "double heart" (Psa 12:2); "unite my heart to fear your name" (Psa 86:11); "one heart" (Jer 32:39; 2Ch 30:12; Eze 11:19); "purify your hearts, you double-minded" (Jam 4:8).

17243.text: k. Heart states described through materials [Claude reading on the pattern; the images are the text's]: stone (Eze 11:19; 36:26; Job 41:24; 1Sa 25:37 "his heart died within him, and he became as a stone"); diamond (Zec 7:12); wax, water, melting (Psa 22:14; Jos 7:5; 2Sa 17:10); fat, unfeeling (Psa 119:70); "fattened your hearts" (Jam 5:5); oven (Hos 7:6); deep water (Pro 20:5); a stream of water in God's hand (Pro 21:1); grass struck down and withered (Psa 102:4); burning (Luk 24:32); a mirror: "As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man" (Pro 27:19)

17260.text: b. The human spirit: *Troubled, anxious:* Gen 41:8; Dan 2:1, 3; 7:15 ("my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me"); Joh 13:21; 2Co 2:13.; *Revived:*; after eating ("his spirit revived" 1Sa 30:12); after drinking ("his spirit returned, and he revived" Judg 15:19); on good news (Gen 45:27); *Broken, crushed:* Exo 6:9 ("broken spirit and harsh slavery"); Pro 15:4, 13; 17:22; 18:14 ("A man's spirit will endure sickness, but a crushed spirit who can bear?"); Job 17:1; Psa 34:18; 51:17.; *Faint, failing:* Psa 77:3; 142:3; 143:4, 7; Isa 57:16; 61:3.; *Lowly, contrite vs proud, haughty:* Isa 57:15; 66:2; Pro 16:18–19; 29:23; Ecc 7:8; Mat 5:3 ("poor in spirit").; *Governed or ungoverned:* "he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Pro 16:32); "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecc 7:9).; *Weighed by God:* "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Pro 16:2).; *Knowing and understanding:*; "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8); "out of my understanding a spirit answers me" (Job 20:3); "the spirit within me constrains me" (Job 32:18); "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1Co 2:11) — [Claude reading] the spirit as the person's self-knowledge.; *Distinct from "mind" (nous) in prayer:* "my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful … I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also" (1Co 14:14–15); "be renewed in the spirit of your minds" (Eph 4:23).; *Jesus' spirit:* "perceiving in his spirit" (Mar 2:8); "sighed deeply in his spirit" (Mar 8:12); "deeply moved in his spirit" (Joh 11:33); "troubled in his spirit" (Joh 13:21); "yielded up his spirit" (Mat 27:50; Joh 19:30; Luk 23:46).; *Paul's spirit:* "his spirit was provoked within him" (Act 17:16); "my spirit was not at rest" (2Co 2:13); "refreshed my spirit" (1Co 16:18); "I serve with my spirit" (Rom 1:9).; *Fervent:* "fervent in spirit" (Rom 12:11; Act 18:25); "grew and became strong in spirit" (Luk 1:80).; *Stirred by God:*; "the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus" (2Ch 36:22; Ezr 1:1); "everyone whose spirit God had stirred" (Ezr 1:5); the spirit of Zerubbabel (Hag 1:14); of Pul (1Ch 5:26); of the Medes (Jer 51:11); *Hardened by God:* "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deu 2:30).

17266.text: a. Hebrew flesh: the whole visible, related, mortal person: *Body and meat:* the purity law (Lev 13–16), sacrifices, "meat" in the wilderness (Num 11) and in cooking.; *Kin:*; "we are your bone and flesh" (2Sa 5:1; Gen 29:14); "he is our brother, our own flesh" (Gen 37:27); "not to hide yourself from your own flesh" (Isa 58:7); "close relative" (Lev 18:6; 25:49, H7607); "one flesh" (Gen 2:24; Mat 19:5–6; Mar 10:8; Eph 5:31); *"All flesh" = every living being / humankind:* Gen 6:12–13; Isa 40:5–6 ("All flesh is grass"); Jer 32:27 ("the God of all flesh"); "the God of the spirits of all flesh" (Num 16:22; 27:16).; *Frailty in contrast to God:*; "What can flesh do to me?" (Psa 56:4); "an arm of flesh" (2Ch 32:8); "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5); "their horses are flesh, and not spirit" (Isa 31:3); "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh" (Gen 6:3); *Flesh responding to the inner seat:*; "My flesh trembles for fear of you" (Psa 119:120); "shuddering seizes my flesh" (Job 21:6); "the hair of my flesh stood up" when a spirit glided past (Job 4:15) — spirit → flesh; "my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you" (Psa 63:1); "my heart and flesh sing for joy" (Psa 84:2); "my heart is glad … my flesh also dwells secure" (Psa 16:9; Act 2:26); "My flesh and my heart may fail" (Psa 73:26); "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh" (Pro 14:30); "they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh" (Pro 4:22); "There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin" (Psa 38:3); "much study is a weariness of the flesh" (Ecc 12:12); "Ahab … put sackcloth on his flesh" (1Ki 21:27); *Heart of flesh vs heart of stone:* "I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Eze 11:19; 36:26). Here *flesh* is the good state of the heart: responsive, living.; *Life is in the blood of the flesh:* "the life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11, 14; Gen 9:4; Deu 12:23).

17273.text: 3.3 Unity and division: *Unity:*; "unite my heart" (Psa 86:11); "one heart" (Jer 32:39; Eze 11:19; 2Ch 30:12); "one heart and soul" (Act 4:32); "one spirit, with one mind" (Phili 1:27); "one flesh" (Gen 2:24); "he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him" (1Co 6:17); *Division:*; "double heart" (Psa 12:2); "double-minded" (Jam 4:8); "his heart was not wholly true" (1Ki 11:4; 15:3); "not with a whole heart" (2Ch 25:2); "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Mat 26:41); "the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit … to keep you from doing the things you want to do" (Gal 5:17); [Claude reading] Division *within* a person is described as a split heart or as spirit against flesh. Union *between* persons uses the same terms (one heart, one soul, one flesh, one spirit).

17274.text: 3.4 Distinction — where the text separates the components: *Division of soul and spirit (Heb 4:12):* "piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart." [Claude reading] Soul and spirit are close enough that only the word of God can separate them, just as joints and marrow are adjacent parts of the body. The heart is where the *thoughts and intentions* are, and they are *discerned* there.; *Living soul vs life-giving spirit:* "The first man Adam became a living being [psychē]; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit" (1Co 15:45; cf. Gen 2:7).; *Spirit vs mind:* 1Co 14:14–15 (above).; *Spirit vs flesh (as kind):*; "a spirit does not have flesh and bones" (Luk 24:39); "horses are flesh, and not spirit" (Isa 31:3); "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (Joh 3:6); "the flesh is no help at all" (Joh 6:63); "put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit" (1Pe 3:18; 4:6); "the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved" (1Co 5:5); *Soul vs body:* "cannot kill the soul" (Mat 10:28).; *Spirit vs body in place:* "absent in body, … present in spirit" (1Co 5:3–4; Col 2:5). fringe [Claude reading]: the spirit can be "with" people where the body is not.; *Inner vs outer:*; "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2Co 4:16, with "lose heart"); "a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit" (Rom 2:29); "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4); "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1Sa 16:7); "what is in the heart" vs "outward appearance" (2Co 5:12); *Food and the heart:* "since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled" (Mar 7:19). The text draws a boundary: food goes to the stomach, not the heart. But see §3.6, where food *does* strengthen the heart.

17278.text: 3.7 Containment — what is placed "in" what: *In the heart:*; law, words, commandments (Deu 6:6; Psa 37:31; 119:11; Jer 31:33); wisdom (Pro 2:10; 14:33); fear of God (Jer 32:40); eternity (Ecc 3:11); idols (Eze 14:3); deceit (Pro 12:20); folly (Pro 22:15); anger (Ecc 7:9); the Spirit (2Co 1:22; Gal 4:6); Christ "may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Eph 3:17); "the peace of Christ rule in your hearts" (Col 3:15); "the word of Christ dwell in you richly … thankfulness in your hearts" (Col 3:16); God's love "poured into our hearts" (Rom 5:5); what "the devil had already put into the heart of Judas" (Joh 13:2); what "God has put into their hearts" (Rev 17:17; Neh 2:12; 7:5; Ezr 7:27; 2Co 8:16); *Within me:* spirit (Psa 143:4; Isa 26:9; Job 32:18; Dan 7:15); soul (Psa 42:5–6; 131:2); heart (Psa 22:14; 39:3; 109:22; Jer 8:18; 23:9; Lam 1:20; Hos 11:8).; *Spirit and heart inside flesh:* "I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh" (Eze 36:26); "put breath in you" (Eze 37:6).; *Spirit and body:* "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1Co 6:19); "if the Spirit … dwells in you, he … will also give life to your mortal bodies" (Rom 8:11).; [Claude reading] The heart is the innermost *location* in the text's picture. Soul-states, spirit, God's Spirit, words, law and dispositions are placed "in" it. Spirit and soul are also spoken of as "within me", but they are less often described as containers.

17287.text: d. Missing from M47, but clearly inner-seat vocabulary in the English text: kidneys ("heart and mind", Jer 11:20 etc.); bowels / stomach (Lam 1:20); *nous* "mind" (1Co 14:14; Rom 7:25; Eph 4:23; brief §4 says M15); "inner being / inner self" (Eph 3:16; 2Co 4:16); "bones" (repeatedly paired with heart and spirit); "compassion" (Hos 11:8); [verify] which clusters hold these.

19602.text: 2 Samuel 6:21: "and I will celebrate before the Lord": The chapter is the bringing up of the ark. It opens in celebration: *"David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord, with songs and lyres"* (v5). Then Uzzah takes hold of the ark and *"the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah"* (v7). David's inner state turns three times in three verses: *"David was angry because the Lord had broken out against Uzzah"* (v8); *"David was afraid of the Lord that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the Lord come to me?""* (v9); *"So David was not willing to take the ark of the Lord into the city of David"* (v10); What brings him back is hearing that *"The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom"* (v12). He brings the ark up *"with rejoicing"*, and *"David danced before the Lord with all his might"* (v14).; Michal sees this from the window and *"she despised him in her heart"* (v16). The contempt is inward first. Her words come out only when he arrives (v20). Her measure is the eyes of others: *"uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (v20).; David's answer: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the Lord—and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (v21). "Celebrate" is the same word as *"celebrating"* in v5 (H7832). The celebration that stopped at Uzzah's death has come back, and David names the ground: he was chosen. He also names before whom he celebrates. Michal spoke of the servants' eyes. David speaks of the Lord.; He does not defend his dignity. He goes further: *"I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes"* (v22). He accepts being lowered in her eyes. Her contempt does not move him, because he answers to a different measure.; The choosing is set against Michal's own house: *"above your father and above all his house"*. I read the reply as answering her contempt with the fact of the choosing. The verse names the house of Saul directly. The chapter closes on Michal: *"Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death"* (v23). The text does not give a cause.

19604.text: Psalm 65:4: "We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house": The psalm opens with prayer and with sin: *"O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come"* (v2); *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (v3); The verse comes straight after the atoning: *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (v4). Being chosen is set with being brought near and dwelling. The response is satisfaction (H7646), and what satisfies is *"the goodness of your house"*. The satisfaction is not in the chosen person; it is in what is in God's house.; The speaker moves from *"me"* (v3) to *"we"* (v4). The one chosen is spoken of in the singular, and the satisfaction is spoken in the plural.; The psalm then widens beyond the chosen. God is *"the hope of all the ends of the earth"* (v5), and *"those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs"* (v8). The land itself is given voice at the end: *"they shout and sing together for joy"* (v13). The joy of the chosen in v4 is one part of a psalm that ends with all of creation rejoicing. The verse does not say the chosen have the joy alone.

19609.text: Isaiah 44:2: "Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen": The chapter opens directly after a threat: *"deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling"* (43:28). Then: *"But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen!"* (44:1). The "fear not" comes right after the words of destruction.; The ground of not fearing is who the Lord is to the one chosen: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (v2). He made, he formed, he will help, and he has chosen. The chosen person is not told to be brave. He is told who has chosen him.; What follows is given to the chosen one's offspring, and it reaches the inner being: *"I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants"* (v3); *"This one will say, 'I am the Lord's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The Lord's'"* (v5); Those who are chosen come to name themselves as belonging to him.; The "fear not" comes again with a second ground: *"Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses!"* (v8). The second ground is having been told.; The idol-maker in the same chapter has no such ground. He cuts the wood himself and then prays to it: *"Deliver me, for you are my god!"* (v17). The text says *"he cannot deliver himself"* (v20). The chosen one is told: *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (v21), and *"return to me, for I have redeemed you"* (v22).

19639.text: Isaiah 58:5: "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?": Here the inner act is what is weighed by God's choosing. The chapter opens on people who look devout: *"Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness … they delight to draw near to God"* (v2); *"'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?'"* (v3); The answer is about what is going on alongside the fast: *"Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers. Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist"* (v3–4).; Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?"* (v5).; "Humble himself" in v5 is *ʿānâ* (*to afflict*; H6031B) with the soul (H5315I), the same phrase as *"humbled ourselves"* in v3. The self-humbling of the soul is what they offered. God asks whether that is what he chooses.; What he does choose is turned outward: *"Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry … and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?"* (v6–7).; "Delight" in v2 (twice) is *ḥāpēṣ* (H2654A). It is the same word as *"chose that in which I did not delight"* in Isaiah 66:4, read in §2a. In v3 *"your own pleasure"* is the noun from the same root (H2656).

19679.text: 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me": Barzillai had fed David in his flight. He came with others bringing *"honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat"*, saying *"The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness"* (17:27, 29). When David returns, the king offers him a place at court: *"Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem"* (19:33).; Barzillai declines, and his reason is about his own inner capacity: *"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"* (v35). The Hebrew is "know between good and evil" (H3045 with H0996, H2896B, H7451A). It is the same pairing as Isaiah 7:15–16, *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. Here it is the knowing of taste and pleasure, and Barzillai says that at eighty it has gone. The same words, put to the palate rather than to right and wrong, mark a change of face (#1919).; He makes his choice, and it is for someone else: *"Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city … But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you"* (v37).; The king hands the choosing back to Barzillai: *"Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (v38). *"Whatever seems good to you"* is literally "the good in your eyes" (H2896A, H5869). *"all that you desire of me"* is the choosing verb (H0977): "all that you choose of me". So the old man who says he can no longer tell good from bad on his palate is given the king's word that what is good in his eyes will be done.; The outcome is told: *"the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home"* (v39); *"Chimham went on with him"* (v40).

19683.text: Acts 15:22, 25 — "it seemed good … having come to one accord, to choose men": The choosing ends a dispute that went to the heart of the faith. Some taught *"Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved"* (v1), and there was *"no small dissension and debate"* (v2).; At the council the first word about choosing is God's. Peter says *"Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (v7). It is the same verb as the church's later choosing (G1586). He goes on: *"God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit … having cleansed their hearts by faith"* (v8–9). The assembly *"fell silent"* and *"listened"* (v12). James gives his judgement from the prophets (v13–21).; Then the church chooses: *"it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch"* (v22). The letter says how they came to it: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you"* (v25). "One accord" (G3661) is a single shared mind. The same verb for "seemed good" (G1380) then joins them to the Spirit: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (v28).; So the church's choosing: follows God's choosing, in the same verb; follows listening in silence; comes from one accord; is joined to what seemed good to the Holy Spirit; The outcome is in the hearers' hearts: *"when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement"* (v31). Judas and Silas *"encouraged and strengthened the brothers"* (v32), and were *"sent off in peace"* (v33). The letter answers the *"unsettling"* of their *"minds"* (v24).

19884.text: "To know between good and evil."; It is the knowing that grounds the moral choice (Isa 7:15–16).; It is the palate's knowing of pleasant and unpleasant, which fades at eighty (2Sa 19:35).; It is the weighing of words in a dispute (Job 34:3–4).; *Why:* the same knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste, and to judgement.

20285.text: Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened": Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers: *"By no means!"* (v1). *"God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew"* (v2). He gives Elijah, who thought he was alone, and God's reply: *"I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal"* (v4). *"So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"* (v5–6).; Then v7: *"What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"*.; The others are *"the rest"*. Two things are said of them: They were seeking (*epizēteō*, G1934) and did not obtain.; They were hardened (*pōroō*, G4456).; The hardening is described from Scripture: *"God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day"* (v8). The giving is God's act (rule 72, A). The eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear are in the human inner being.; Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

20286.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: Those who are not among the chosen are described as seeking and not obtaining.; They were hardened: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear (v8).; The hardening is not the end. Their stumbling is not *"in order that they might fall"* (v11).; Jealousy is named as an aim: *"so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11).; The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not by works (v5–6). The verse says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

20287.text: 1 Thessalonians 1:4: "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you": Paul writes of what he remembers of them: *"your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v3). Then: *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (v4–5).; "Know" is *oida* (G6063). Here another person knows that someone has been chosen. The ESV joins v4 to v5 with "because": the knowing rests on how the gospel came to them. The passage goes on to what was seen in them: *"you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit"* (v6); *"you became an example to all the believers"* (v7); *"your faith in God has gone forth everywhere"* (v8); *"you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven"* (v9–10)

20304.text: Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

20305.text: Job 34:4 — Elihu: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good": Elihu is angry with both sides. He *"burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God"*, and at the friends *"because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong"* (32:2–3).; He calls the listeners to weigh Job's case together, and calls that weighing a choosing: *"Hear my words, you wise men"* … *"for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food"*; *"Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good"* (v2–4). The choosing here is not of a course of life. It is a judgement: picking out what is right in the case before them.; The picture is tasting. The ear tests (H0974) as the palate tastes (H2938). Then *"let us know among ourselves what is good"* uses the same words as Barzillai's *"Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not"* (2Sa 19:35): know (H3045), between (H0996), good (H2896). Barzillai said the palate's knowing had gone with age. Elihu uses the palate as the picture for weighing words.; What they are to weigh is Job's own claim. Elihu quotes it: *"I am in the right, and God has taken away my right"* (v5). He judges it at once: *"What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water"*, *"who travels in company with evildoers"* (v7–8). His ground is God's justice: *"far be it from God that he should do wickedness"* (v10); *"his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps"* (v21).

20312.text: The weighing is itself a choosing. *"Let us choose what is right"* (34:4) is a judgement made together, by testing words as the palate tastes food. It uses the same words as Barzillai's knowing between good and bad by taste (2Sa 19:35).

21311.text: Called here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21313.text: Called is here the outward act of summoning, addressing or sending for another person or thing; it bears on the other's response but names no inner-being operation of the one who calls.

21314.text: Called is the standing given by God's call (the vocation); it is what diligence, worthiness or walking is directed at, not an inner operation in itself.

21359.text: Offer here is the ritual or narrated presenting of an offering, a prescribed or reported act with no inner-being operation named by it.
